With the Lacedaemonians, however, or the Athenians, if you wish to compare yourselves, I grant it — those of that time, when one of those like you might reasonably be compared with them.

127. For it is not reasonable that the athlete still ambitious and not yet yielding in strength should challenge the sick of those renowned in his time, nor the dead, but, if there be any in vigour, to contend with them for victory; and if not, to seek to do some such thing as will show him weaker than none of the former. This, then, is the sound argument about such matters. But if indeed something must be granted, examine the matter neither comparing it with those of that time, who were the mightiest, nor with those now, who differ in nothing from the basest, but with the middling among them or even those still less than these.

128. Among the Athenians, then, especially in the time of Philip, when they had yielded the leadership and clung only to freedom that remained, a certain Leptines introduced a law that it was necessary to take away the immunities from those who held them from the people, except those descended from Harmodius and Aristogeiton, and that henceforth it should no longer be allowed to give anyone this gift. What then? Is there any way they accepted the law? Surely not, but it was convicted on indictment.

129. Come then, compare this custom with that law, and if it appear to you in any way better, keep it and make it stronger for the future — which would of necessity come about, if it be not now dissolved; but if, considering it in every way, you find it worse, imitate the Athenians of that time, and the thing that is more absurd than what was then dissolved by them, do you now too dissolve.

130. The showing the city false and untrustworthy about its gifts, and the wronging of benefactors by robbing them of their requitals, and all such things, attach equally and in common to both; but there it was not possible that those who had held the immunity should have profited nothing; for what they acquired from the remission remained to them entirely, since for the rest of the time too they were going to be more prosperous through it. But to those robbed of the image, from having been honoured before, nothing whatever remains, save the outrage and the dishonour.

131. And besides, the one who then proposed the law accused some of those who had received the immunity and declared the most of them wicked, not merely unworthy of gratitude; so that this was the dreadful thing, that, not accusing all, he robbed all of the gifts. But here it is not even possible for those who take them away to say anything against those men; for whom they do not even know, how is it possible to accuse them?

132. And further, the law made certain ones exempt, those reputed to have most benefited the city, the descendants of Harmodius and Aristogeiton; but here there is nothing exempt. For by the matter being done without record, and forbidden about nothing at all either by law or by decree, it is possible for it to befall anyone, against whomever it may seem good to the general.

133. And indeed the law seemed to do a dreadful thing in taking away from the people their authority, so that it should not even henceforth be possible to vote this gift. And how much better to prevent the people from the outset from giving anything, if it were not advantageous to the city, than, leaving them the granting, to make the taking-away rest with one man? For, it being shameful, as no one would gainsay, to rob the recipients of anything, by the law this happened once, but by the custom it occurs always.

134. And indeed, if it seems grievous that the city should be robbed of any authority, you too rob yourselves of the authority of guarding secure the things given to the recipients. For to whomever you give the honour, it is no longer in your power to let him keep it; rather one man is always master of this, the one serving as general. And yet it is worse for it not to be in your power through custom than through what is forbidden by law. For those people have not in a manner been robbed of the authority over what they have forbidden themselves to do by law, but withdrew willingly because of the advantage.

135. But in the case of the custom it is not even possible to say this, that they have robbed themselves, if indeed, of that about which they neither judged nor deliberated. And indeed there they had some consolation in the equality and commonness of the matter, all alike being robbed of their immunities; but among you whoever chances is robbed of the image, and often the better. And further, there the law robbed the holder not that another might receive, but among you it is for this very cause, which is altogether more grievous than merely to be robbed.

136. And indeed this at least no one is ignorant of, doubtless — how much harder it seems to suffer something through another than through oneself. So then by the law it came about, that some might not have the immunities, of which he spoke as unworthy, that the rest should give them up; but by the custom among you, that others might receive, the holders are robbed.

137. And altogether this is heavier for those who suffer. If, then, on the cases where it is most necessary, one should wish to see whom this custom wrongs and whom that law was going to grieve — having taken away from those who not only had immunity, but had also obtained the image — let him so consider the rest of each. For these in a manner suffered nothing; for what they had received in the way of an addition, this they lost, the greater gift being preserved to them; but in the case of the others the argument would be equal. But the matter is plain, I think, even of itself; for by how much the image is greater than the immunity, by so much better are those who obtained it; and the argument would become still plainer thus:

138. for the immunity makes the recipients more prosperous, and those most desire it who have been eager about money; but the image has only the august and the honourable. By how much, then, we should all say better are those who choose to benefit some for nothing and rather for the sake of repute than those who do so for money and for gain's sake, by so much I should say that this custom not only wrongs better men, but also prevents you from being benefited by better men than the law prevented those people.

139. But I, for my part, am at a loss why ever you do not even set up a law about this, by which it shall be for the future, if indeed it pleases you. By Zeus, for such a law lying in the city brings no small shame. Then what you consider shameful to write, is it not shameful to do? And how much better not to use any of the things badly written than to do them? Or which would you call better — those so disposed toward absurd things as to abstain even from things granted, or those who do things not even conceded?

140. But I, for my part, would say — it being agreed that one ought in no way to do anything unjust or unseemly — that among those by whom such a thing is done by law, there would be less ground for accusation than among those by whom it is done by custom. For first, the law is express, and could never become worse; for it is possible neither to take away from nor add to what is written; but the custom, if it be base, must of necessity become ever baser too, by not being comprehended nor defined.

141. I mean, for instance, they say this took its beginning straightway from those broken down and no longer even standing on their bases; for these the generals used, repairing them and in a manner making them anew, then — what was left — those sound but having no inscriptions were inscribed; and for the rest now even some of the inscribed, the very ancient ones; for let what they say be true: afterward there must of necessity be no distinction; for in other matters too it is so — expense, disorder, luxury;

142. you will never find any of the worse customs standing still or remaining the same, until it be altogether prevented. For through admitting addition always, and through being unexaminable by a little and not readily appearing to anyone how much one thing is worse than another, it advances to the utmost, just as, I think, some of the sores and diseases which are by nature apt to grow from anything. And besides this there is that point too: those who do something base by law do it not as being such, but having been deceived; but those who do base things by custom all would say err knowingly, things which do not even seem to themselves fit to have been written.

143. Do not, then, if it began earlier and more time has passed, on this account think it less fitting for you to abolish it; for those who guard such things incur no less shame than those who introduced them, but on the contrary are the more liable to those wishing to accuse them. For when first done, it was not even impossible for it to escape the men of that time, and that too while those doing it were still on their guard; but what has come about for a long time, no one can be ignorant of, especially since this pretext has been altogether removed for you, who sit in judgment about this very thing. As, then, if it were necessary for you to begin one of the noble things, you would not on this account hesitate, likewise it is reasonable, even if it be necessary to abolish one of the base things.

144. Do not, then, let time benefit the custom, if indeed it is bad, as I think I made plain long ago. For not, if it has harmed you for a long time, on this account, I think, is it fitting that it never cease harming. For neither, having taken a wicked man from of old, will you release him for the sake of the time he passed being wicked. Nor again, if one could heal a disease that long troubled him, would he spare to be from the outset in health.

145. And I think that you, if one of the gods should make plain to you the thing about to grieve the city again at some time, would altogether guard against this, it being in your power; then will you not neglect the thing that will harm others, since it will be afterward, but will allow the thing that wrongs you yourselves most greatly, because it began earlier? This, then, is altogether simple, if anyone thinks one ought never to prevent what is done customarily but absurdly.

146. I think it fitting that you reflect rather on this, that, while there are many things in the city on all of which you reasonably pride yourselves — first the laws and the good order about the constitution, on which you are most ambitious, then, I think, such things as temples, theatres, dockyards, walls, harbours, of which some display wealth and magnanimity and the greatness of your former power, others your piety toward the gods — you take pleasure in none less than in the multitude of the statues, and reasonably;

147. for such a thing not only brings adornment, like any other of the dedications, but also displays not least the strength of the city and its character. For chance persons are neither benefited by many, nor willing, nor perhaps able, to honour many. And besides there is that point too: for not only on this account has it come about that there are most statues among you, but also, I think, because the Romans, though often taking from everywhere the furnishings of temples and palaces, have never moved any of those among you;

148. seeing that even Nero, having so great a desire and zeal about this, that he abstained neither from those of Olympia nor from those of Delphi — though he honoured these temples above all — and besides transferred the most of those from the acropolis at Athens and many of those from Pergamum, although that precinct belonged to him — for about those among others, what need to speak? — those among you alone he let be, and showed so great goodwill and honour toward you at once, that he judged the whole city more sacred than the foremost temples.

149. For you know that Acratus who went round well-nigh the whole inhabited world for this purpose and passed by not even one village, that he came here too. And, you being grieved, as is likely, he said he was present to view; for he had no authority to touch any of the things here. Therefore, apart from the common adornment of the sight, the multitude of the images procures you another repute too. For these appear a proof of your friendship toward the rulers and of the regard from them.

150. Then the Romans and Nero so guarded the things among you and judged them august; and will you not guard them? And Nero, the most violent of emperors, granting himself the most and considering all things less in face of all authority, robbed no one of the image among those honoured by the Rhodians alone; but do you yourselves rob them? And how much better it would have been for the same to have happened here too. For among the others the names of those honoured remain, and no one would wipe out the inscriptions; but you, as though you had suffered some evil from them, cut them out.

151. And yet one might say that even if they were taken away by the kings, not even so are the men wronged. For not as going to give them to others, but needing them for adornment, they transferred them, so that none of them would take away the name, nor again would they fare worse, being set up, instead of in the market of Megara and Epidaurus and Andros or Myconos, in the temples of the Romans. And even if one set this aside, it would have been better, so far as you are concerned, for their honours to have been thus obliterated. For there would have been no error of yours, nor would you yourselves have wronged your own benefactors and the heroes, but, if anything, would have been wronged along with them.

152. And indeed, if one of you should ask — even if it will seem rather ridiculous — why ever neither you nor anyone else makes the images of those judged worthy of this gift of clay, it being doubtless easier and involving no expense or an altogether small one — you would say, I think: not on account of its not being outraged, but also on account of the honours of good men remaining, if possible, forever. Now then know that all your statues are weaker than wax. For one must not consider whether they bear the sun. For they are corrupted by the flattery toward others, and if it seem good to so-and-so and so-and-so for whatever cause, they are no longer the men they were before. And such corruption is far worse.

153. For then the weakness of the material would be convicted, but now the baseness of the city seems to appear. Therefore you give the statues just as those who buy these dolls for their children. For they too give them in such a way as to be in no way grieved when they are broken to pieces a little later. Are you ignorant of the shame attaching to the matter and how much laughter you incur, lying publicly, and that too so openly?

154. For in the decrees, at least, you write: and to set up an image of so-and-so. How, one might say to you, men of Rhodes, do you write to set up the one already standing, if it so happen, five hundred years ago? Then you judge those women who substitute children wicked and think they do a dreadful thing in lying; but you yourselves are not ashamed to do this with the images, both saying that the statues belong to those to whom they do not, and that too not being unacquainted with the jeers against the city?

155. Many, at least, say that the statues of the Rhodians are like the actors. For just as each of these enters now as one character, now as another, so your statues take now one face, now another, and stand all but acting a part. For the same one is now a Greek, now a Roman, and again, if it so happen, a Macedonian or a Persian; and this in some cases so that the one who sees it knows at once. For the dress and the footgear and other such things convict the falsehood.

156. And I omit countless of the things that happen, such as often inscribing the name of some young man on the image of a very old man — you having found, I think, some marvellous gift, if along with the honour you give also the youth; and again, an athlete's statue standing, as belonging to an altogether weak and ordinary man in body. For that so-and-so should be seen among you riding, or engaging an enemy, or marshalling an army, a man who never once touched the ground with his own feet nor came down from the shoulders of those who carried him, is perhaps nothing strange; but so-and-so stands among you boxing.

157. And I say these things, by Zeus, not wishing to be hateful to you nor disparaging the city, but that it may appear to do nothing unworthy of itself nor alien to its other good order and constitution. And it seems to me one might reasonably be moved, through goodwill toward all the Greeks, not only toward you, if anything here be not well, to speak and reveal it. For formerly the common dignity was made up of many, and many exalted Greece — you, the Athenians, the Lacedaemonians, the Thebans, for some time the Corinthians, of old the Argives. But now the matter of the others is nothing.

158. For some of them are utterly abolished and perished, and others behave unbecomingly, doing such things as you hear, and in every way obliterating their ancient repute, the fools thinking they live luxuriously and counting it gain that no one prevents them from erring. But you remain; for to you alone it belongs to seem really to have been somebody and not to be utterly despised. For on account of those who so treat their own fatherlands, as some say truly, nothing prevented all the Greeks from having long ago become more dishonoured than the Phrygians or Thracians.

159. As, then, of a prosperous and great house left desolate, when one heir still remains, in him are all things, and if he err in anything and is ill spoken of, he obliterates the whole repute of the house and shames all the former ones; so your affairs now stand toward Greece. For do not think you are first of it, men of Rhodes, do not think it. For it is possible to be first of the living and of those who perceive honour or dishonour; but her things are gone and in every way shamefully and pitiably corrupted; nor is it possible any longer to conceive the preeminence and brilliance of the cities, looking at least to the men.

160. But the stones rather display the august and the greatness of Greece, and the ruins of the buildings; since the very inhabitants and those who manage public affairs one would not even call descendants of Mysians; so that to me, at least, the cities utterly abolished seem to fare better than those so inhabited. For the memory of these remains sound, and the name is outraged through none of the former noble things; just as, I think, of the dead too it is altogether better that the bodies be made away with and that no one see them than that they appear rotting.

161. And these things perhaps came to me more than was reasonable, when I mentioned the whole state. But that I wished to make plain to you, that you are left alone of the Greeks to whom one might both give counsel and about whom there is still ground to be grieved when they seem to err. Reasonably, then, you would give heed to yourselves and examine all such things more exactly than your ancestors. For to them, in many other things, belonged the display of virtue — in presiding over the rest, in aiding the wronged, in acquiring allies, in founding cities, in conquering in war;

162. but for you it is not possible to do any such thing, but there is left, I think, to preside over yourselves and to administer the city, and to honour someone and applaud not in the manner of the many, and to deliberate and to judge and to sacrifice to the gods and to keep festival; in all of which it is possible to appear better than the others. Therefore such things of yours too meet with praise, and are recognized among all as not small — the walk, the haircut, that no one swaggers through the city, but is compelled through your custom that even the strangers visiting walk in an orderly way; just as, I think, one may see even the rustics, when they come to a wrestling-school or gymnasium, move less without rhythm;

163. and besides this the manner of the dress, the thing that would perhaps appear ridiculous to someone, the measure of the purple; and the more conspicuous things now — the watching in quiet, the clucking of the tongue; all these make the city august, through these you seem to differ from the rest, for all these you are admired, loved. The harbours, the walls, the dockyards adorn you less than the ancient and Greek quality in your customs — that when one comes to be among you, straightway, on disembarking, he knows, even if he happen to be a barbarian, that he is not come to some city of Syria or Cilicia; but among others, unless one hear the name of the place, say, that it is called Lyceum or Academy, there is no difference.

164. For what cause, then, do I say these things, now ceasing, and wishing to make what plain? That by so much the more you ought to be ambitious and pass over none of the things that happen. And if you are thus disposed in all that you do, perhaps you will seem in no way worse than your ancestors. For to preserve oneself in such a state and to remain in the posture of virtue seems to me marvellous;

165. just as, I think, one may see among those sailing, when a storm has fallen or the wind is violent, not even the most wanton of them doing anything shameful, but being intent only on the sailing, while in calm the insolence of both the sailors and the passengers comes to the surface, even if they be not licentious; in the same way, I think, war is wont to rouse and master even the baser sort, but in so great peace and ease it belongs to the best men to be carried into no shame nor disorder.
